BACKGROUND
Nerandomilast (BI 1015550) is an orally administered preferential inhibitor of phos-
phodiesterase 4B with antifibrotic and immunomodulatory effects. In a phase 2 trial 
involving patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, treatment with nerandomi-
last stabilized lung function over a period of 12 weeks.
METHODS
In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with idiopathic 
pulmonary fibrosis in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive nerandomilast at a dose of 18 mg 
twice daily, nerandomilast at a dose of 9 mg twice daily, or placebo, with stratifi-
cation according to background antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib or pirfenidone vs. 
none). The primary end point was the absolute change from baseline in forced vital 
capacity (FVC), measured in milliliters, at week 52.
RESULTS
A total of 1177 patients underwent randomization, of whom 77.7% were taking 
nintedanib or pirfenidone at enrollment. Adjusted mean changes in FVC at week 
52 were −114.7 ml (95% confidence interval [CI], −141.8 to −87.5) in the neran-
domilast 18-mg group, −138.6 ml (95% CI, −165.6 to −111.6) in the nerandomilast 
9-mg group, and −183.5 ml (95% CI, −210.9 to −156.1) in the placebo group. The 
adjusted difference between the nerandomilast 18-mg group and the placebo 
group was 68.8 ml (95% CI, 30.3 to 107.4; P<0.001), and the adjusted difference 
between the nerandomilast 9-mg group and the placebo group was 44.9 ml (95% 
CI, 6.4 to 83.3; P = 0.02). The most frequent adverse event in the nerandomilast 
groups was diarrhea, reported in 41.3% of the 18-mg group and 31.1% of the 9-mg 
group, as compared with 16.0% in the placebo group. Serious adverse events were 
balanced across trial groups.
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, treatment with nerandomilast re-
sulted in a smaller decline in the FVC than placebo over a period of 52 weeks. 
(Funded by Boehringer Ingelheim; FIBRONEER-IPF ClinicalTrials.gov number, 
NCT05321069.)

I
diopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a 
fibrosing interstitial lung disease character-
ized by progressive decline in lung function.1 
The pathogenesis of IPF is thought to involve aber-
rant wound repair in response to alveolar injury, 
leading to a self-sustaining fibrotic process.2 Two 
antifibrotic drugs, nintedanib and pirfenidone, 
slow decline in lung function in patients with IPF3,4 
and have become the standard of care.1 However, 
these drugs do not halt progression, and their 
gastrointestinal side effects often prevent treat-
ment initiation or result in discontinuation.3-6 
There remains a need for effective, well-tolerated 
drugs for IPF that can be used as monotherapy or 
in combination with other therapies to preserve 
lung function.
Nerandomilast (BI 1015550) is an orally ad-
ministered preferential inhibitor of phosphodies-
terase 4B. In preclinical models of lung fibrosis, 
nerandomilast showed antifibrotic and immuno-
modulatory effects.7,8 In a phase 2 trial involving 
147 patients with IPF, nerandomilast at a dose of 
18 mg twice daily stabilized lung function over 
a period of 12 weeks, with acceptable safety.9 We 
conducted the phase 3 FIBRONEER-IPF trial to 
investigate the efficacy and safety of nerandomi-
last at a dose of 9 mg twice daily or 18 mg twice 
daily, as monotherapy or with background antifi-
brotic therapy, in patients with IPF.
Methods
Trial Design and Oversight
The FIBRONEER-IPF trial was a double-blind, 
randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted 
at 332 sites in 36 countries.10 The trial was car-
ried out in compliance with the protocol (avail-
able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org) 
and in accordance with the principles of the 
Declaration of Helsinki, the Harmonised Tripar-
tite Guideline for Good Clinical Practice from 
the International Council for Harmonisation, 
applicable regulatory requirements, and stan-
dard operating procedures. Patients provided 
written informed consent before entry into the 
trial. The trial was designed by the steering 
committee (members are listed in the Supple-
mentary Appendix, available at NEJM.org) and 
the sponsor, Boehringer Ingelheim. Data were 
gathered by the investigators (listed in the Sup-
plementary Appendix). All the authors had ac-
cess to the data, which were analyzed by statisti-
cians at Boehringer Ingelheim. The authors vouch 
for the completeness and accuracy of the data. All 
the authors were involved in drafting the manu-
script. Writing assistance, funded by Boehringer 
Ingelheim, was provided by Fleishman-Hillard, 
UK, following guidance from the authors. The 
steering committee decided to submit the manu-
script for publication. Boehringer Ingelheim re-
viewed the manuscript for medical and scientific 
accuracy and intellectual property.
Patients
The first patient was screened on October 6, 2022, 
and the last patient completed the week 52 visit on 
August 16, 2024. Eligible patients were 40 years 
of age or older and had IPF, a forced vital capacity 
(FVC) of at least 45% of the predicted value, and a 
diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monox-
ide (DLCO) of at least 25% of the predicted value. 
IPF was diagnosed by the investigator according to 
guidelines,1 on the basis of a high-resolution com-
puted tomographic (CT) scan obtained no more 
than 12 months before screening. A usual inter-
stitial pneumonia (UIP) or probable UIP pattern 
on high-resolution CT was confirmed by central 
review. Patients with an indeterminate pattern 
on high-resolution CT or a pattern suggesting 
an alternative diagnosis could participate if IPF 
was confirmed locally on the basis of historical 
surgical lung biopsy or cryobiopsy.
Patients who were receiving nintedanib or pir-
fenidone needed to have taken a stable dose for at 
least 12 weeks. Patients who had not received an-
tifibrotic therapy for at least 8 weeks were eligible 
to participate; these patients could initiate ninted­
anib or pirfenidone in the event of IPF progres-
sion, acute exacerbation, or both after 12 weeks of 
the trial. Prednisone at a dose of more than 15 mg 
per day or equivalent for respiratory reasons, not 
permitted at enrollment, could be prescribed dur-
ing the trial for suspected acute exacerbation. Key 
exclusion criteria are listed in the Supplementary 
Appendix.
Randomization and Follow-up
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio 
to receive nerandomilast at a dose of 18 mg twice 
daily, nerandomilast at a dose of 9 mg twice daily, 
or placebo twice daily with the use of interactive 
response technology. Randomization was strati-
fied according to use of background antifibrotic 
therapy (nintedanib or pirfenidone vs. none). Visits

occurred at baseline; weeks 2, 6, 12, 18, 26, 36, 
44, and 52; and every 12 weeks thereafter. A fol-
low-up visit was performed 7 days after the end of 
the treatment period. Interruption of nerandomi-
last treatment was permitted to manage adverse 
events. Dose reductions and interruptions of back-
ground treatment with nintedanib or pirfenidone 
were recommended to manage adverse events, as 
per product labels. Patients who prematurely dis-
continued nerandomilast were asked to attend 
visits as planned. Here we present data collected 
until the first database lock, which took place 
after the last patient had completed the week 52 
visit. Patients continued the blinded trial regimen 
until the final database lock. Patients who com-
pleted the trial while receiving nerandomilast or 
placebo were eligible to receive open-label neran-
domilast in an extension study.
End Points
The primary end point was the absolute change 
from baseline in FVC at week 52. Spirometry was 
performed with SpiroSphere (Clario) spirometers 
in accordance with the recommendations of the 
American Thoracic Society and European Respira-
tory Society.11 The key secondary end point was a 
first acute exacerbation, hospitalization for a re-
spiratory cause, or death, assessed in a time-to-
event analysis over the duration of the trial. Acute 
exacerbations and hospitalizations for a respira-
tory cause were not adjudicated. Acute exacerba-
tions were defined according to published guide-
lines.12 Other secondary end points were the 
absolute change in the percentage of the pre-
dicted value of the FVC at week 52; the absolute 
change in the percentage of the predicted value 
of the DLCO at week 52; absolute changes in the 
Living with Pulmonary Fibrosis questionnaire13 
dyspnea score, cough score, and fatigue score 
(for which higher scores on a scale of 0 to 100 
indicate worse symptoms) at week 52; and the 
time to acute exacerbation or death, time to hos-
pitalization for a respiratory cause or death, time 
to an absolute decline in the percentage of the 
predicted value of the FVC of more than 10 per-
centage points or death, time to an absolute de-
cline in the percentage of the predicted value of 
the DLCO of more than 15 percentage points or 
death, and time to death over the duration of the 
trial. The DLCO was measured with equipment 
at the site in accordance with recommendations 
from the American Thoracic Society and European 
Respiratory Society.14 The time to initiation of 
supplemental oxygen was a prespecified further 
end point. Plasma concentrations of nerandomi-
last at steady state were determined by means of 
high-performance liquid chromatography with 
tandem mass spectrometry.
Safety was assessed through recording of ad-
verse events and clinical monitoring. Adverse 
events were coded according to the Medical Dic-
tionary for Regulatory Activities, version 27.0. Ad-
verse events of interest for phosphodiesterase 4 
(PDE4) inhibitors, such as vasculitis, depression, 
and suicidality, were assessed.
Statistical Analysis
Analyses were conducted in randomly assigned 
patients who had received at least one dose of 
nerandomilast or placebo. The primary end point 
was analyzed with the use of a mixed model for 
repeated measures, including trial group, base-
line background antifibrotic therapy use (yes or 
no), and continuous fixed effects for baseline 
FVC at each visit as covariates. Missing data were 
handled in the primary analysis under the as-
sumption that they were missing at random ex-
cept that missing values for the change in FVC 
for patients who died before week 52 were re-
placed on the basis of the lowest 10th percentile 
of observed values. Further information on the 
statistical analyses is provided in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix and the statistical analysis plan, 
available with the protocol.
To control the familywise type I error rate at 
5%, a graphical testing procedure15 was used in 
multiple comparisons between nerandomilast at 
a dose of 18 mg twice daily or 9 mg twice daily 
and placebo for the primary and key secondary 
end points (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appen-
dix). Results of the other end points were not 
controlled for multiplicity; the widths of the con-
fidence intervals have not been adjusted for multi-
plicity and may not be used in place of hypothesis 
testing. The sample-size calculation is described 
in the Supplementary Appendix.
Results
Patients
A total of 1177 randomly assigned patients re-
ceived at least one dose of nerandomilast or pla-
cebo (Fig. 1). Baseline characteristics were similar 
across trial groups (Table 1). The mean (±SD) age

of the patients was 70.2±7.7 years, the mean FVC 
was 78.2±17.3% of the predicted value, and the 
mean DLCO was 50.9±16.3% of the predicted 
value. The trial population reflected the charac-
teristics of the general population of patients with 
IPF (Table S1). A total of 915 patients (77.7%) took 
background antifibrotic therapy (535 took nin­
tedanib, and 380 took pirfenidone). The duration 
and doses of background antifibrotic therapy are 
shown in Table S2, and the baseline characteris-
tics of subgroups according to background anti-
fibrotic therapy are shown in Table S3.
Similar percentages of patients in each trial 
group completed 52 weeks of the trial regimen 
(81.1 to 82.7%) (Fig. 1 and Fig. S2) and continued 
the trial regimen until the first database lock 
(Fig. S3). The mean duration of exposure to neran-
domilast or placebo until the first database lock 
was approximately 13 months in each group.
Change in FVC and DLCO
Adjusted mean changes in FVC at week 52 were 
−114.7 ml (95% confidence interval [CI], −141.8 
to −87.5) in patients who received nerandomilast 
at a dose of 18 mg twice daily, −138.6 ml (95% CI, 
−165.6 to −111.6) in those who received ner­
andomilast at a dose of 9 mg twice daily, and 
−183.5 ml (95% CI, −210.9 to −156.1) in those 
who received placebo (Fig. 2A). The adjusted dif-
ference between the nerandomilast 18-mg group 
and the placebo group was 68.8 ml (95% CI, 
30.3 to 107.4; P<0.001), and the adjusted differ-
ence between the nerandomilast 9-mg group and 
the placebo group was 44.9 ml (95% CI, 6.4 to 
83.3; P = 0.02). The FVC curves separated short-
ly after randomization and continued to diverge 
up to week 52 (Fig. S4). Sensitivity analyses to 
assess assumptions made in the primary analysis 
are shown in the Supplementary Appendix.

Among patients not taking background anti-
fibrotic therapy, adjusted mean changes in FVC 
at week 52 were −79.2 ml in the nerandomilast 
18-mg group, −70.4 ml in the nerandomilast 9-mg 
group, and −148.7 ml in the placebo group (Fig. 2B 
and Fig. S5). Among patients taking nintedanib, 
adjusted mean changes in FVC at week 52 were 
−118.5 ml in the nerandomilast 18-mg group, 
−130.7 ml in the nerandomilast 9-mg group, and 
−191.6 ml in the placebo group (Fig. 2C and Fig. 
S6). Among patients taking pirfenidone, adjusted 
mean changes in FVC at week 52 were −133.7 ml 
in the nerandomilast 18-mg group, −201.8 ml in 
the nerandomilast 9-mg group, and −197.0 ml in 
the placebo group (Fig. 2D and Fig. S7).
In prespecified subgroup analyses, the treat-
ment effect of nerandomilast as compared with 
placebo appeared to be generally consistent across 
subgroups, although there did not appear to be an 
effect of nerandomilast at the lower dose in pa-
tients taking pirfenidone (Figs. S8 and S9). Ad-
justed mean absolute changes in the percentage of 
the predicted value of the FVC and of the DLCO at 
week 52 are shown in Table S4.
Patient-Reported Outcomes
Adjusted mean absolute changes in the Living 
with Pulmonary Fibrosis questionnaire dyspnea 
score, cough score, and fatigue score at week 52 
were similar across trial groups. Details are pro-
vided in Figure S10.
Time-to-Event End Points
A first acute exacerbation, hospitalization for a 
respiratory cause, or death (key secondary end 
point) occurred in 85 patients (21.7%) in the ner­
andomilast 18-mg group, 79 patients (20.2%) in 
the nerandomilast 9-mg group, and 80 patients 
(20.4%) in the placebo group. The hazard ratio for 
first acute exacerbation, hospitalization for a res­
piratory cause, or death with nerandomilast as 
compared with the placebo group was 1.17

Adverse Events
The percentages of patients with any adverse 
events and any serious adverse events over a pe-
riod of 52 weeks were similar across trial groups 
(Table 3). The most frequent adverse event was 
diarrhea, reported in 41.3% of the patients in the 
nerandomilast 18-mg group, 31.1% of those in 
the nerandomilast 9-mg group, and 16.0% of 
those in the placebo group. The incidence of diar-
rhea was higher among patients taking back-
ground nintedanib therapy than among those not 
taking background therapy (Table 3). Among the

nerandomilast 9-mg group, and 2% of those in the 
placebo group. Adverse events in patients taking 
background nintedanib therapy and background 
pirfenidone therapy are shown in Table 3.
Over a period of 52 weeks, adverse events led to 
interruption of the trial regimen in 19.4% of the 
patients in the nerandomilast 18-mg group, 18.4% 
of those in the nerandomilast 9-mg group, and 
14.2% of those in the placebo group. Adverse 
events led to permanent discontinuation of the 
trial regimen in 14.0% of the nerandomilast 18-mg 
group, 11.7% of the nerandomilast 9-mg group, 
and 10.7% of the placebo group. The adverse 
event that most frequently led to discontinuation 
of the trial regimen was diarrhea, which led to 
discontinuation in 6.1%, 1.8%, and 0.5% of these 
groups, respectively. Adverse events led to discon-
tinuation of the trial regimen more frequently 
among patients taking background antifibrotic 
therapy than among those not taking such thera-
py across trial groups (Table 3).
The adverse events that were reported up to the 
first database lock were consistent with those re-
ported over a period of 52 weeks (Table S6). There 
were no imbalances between the nerandomilast 
and placebo groups with respect to adverse events 
of interest such as vasculitis, depression, suicidal-
ity, or drug-induced liver injury (Table S7).
Plasma Concentrations of Nerandomilast
Over a period of 26 weeks, mean trough plasma 
concentrations of nerandomilast at pharmacoki-
netic steady state were approximately 50% lower 
among patients taking pirfenidone than among 
those taking nintedanib or those not taking back-
ground antifibrotic therapy. Details are provided 
in Figure S12.
Discussion
The positive findings of the phase 3 FIBRONEER-
IPF trial follow more than a decade of clinical 
research in IPF that yielded largely negative re-
sults. Both the doses of nerandomilast that were 
investigated were associated with a significantly 
smaller decline in the FVC than placebo over a 
period of 52 weeks, which indicates a slowing of

disease progression. Safety data suggested that 
the adverse events that were associated with ne-
randomilast are manageable.
The loss of FVC observed over a period of 
52 weeks in the placebo group of this trial, de-
spite more than three quarters of the patients 
already taking antifibrotic therapy, highlights 
the need for additional therapies for IPF. Neran-
domilast reduced the decline in FVC both in pa-
tients taking background antifibrotic therapy and 
in those not taking such therapy. However, an 
interaction between nerandomilast and pirfeni-
done reduced plasma concentrations of neran-
domilast by approximately 50% in patients tak-
ing pirfenidone and meant that only the 18-mg 
twice-daily dose of nerandomilast appeared to 
effective in these patients. No apparent effect of 
nerandomilast was observed on end points re-
lated to the risk of acute exacerbation, hospital-
ization for a respiratory cause, or death, which 
may partly reflect the inconsistency in reporting 
of end points such as acute exacerbation and hos-
pitalization for a respiratory cause.12,16
The adverse event that was most frequently 
associated with nerandomilast was diarrhea, but 
diarrhea led to permanent discontinuation of ner­
andomilast in fewer than 4% of the patients. Diar-
rhea was more frequent among patients who re-
ceived nerandomilast with background nintedanib 
therapy than among those who received neran-
domilast alone, but the risk of diarrhea attributable 
to nerandomilast was similar in these two groups. 
Adverse events of interest given that nerandomilast 
inhibits PDE4, such as vasculitis,17 depression,18,19 
and suicidality,18 were balanced across trial groups.
Limitations of the trial include that it was not 
powered to evaluate nerandomilast in subgroups 
and that acute exacerbations and hospitalizations 
for a respiratory cause were not adjudicated. The 
duration of follow-up did not allow the effect of 
nerandomilast on long-term mortality to be as-
sessed. Discontinuations, initiations, and changes 
in dose administration of nintedanib and pirfeni-
done may have affected the differences observed 
between the nerandomilast and placebo groups. 
Additional data on FVC decline and adverse events 
in patients who received nerandomilast will be 
provided by the open-label extension study. The ef-
ficacy and safety of nerandomilast in patients with 
progressive pulmonary fibrosis (other than IPF) 
were investigated in the FIBRONEER-ILD trial.20
In the FIBRONEER-IPF trial involving patients 
with IPF, treatment with nerandomilast resulted in 
a smaller decline in the FVC than placebo over a 
period of 52 weeks.
